newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan - more cautious about bank/commerce mix.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan - more cautious about bank/commerce mix.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said Thursday the central bank had turned more cautious about allowing banks and commercial firms to combine and urged Congress to put off consideration of such proposals.
"Any wider authorization of banking and commerce should be postponed while we focus on financial modernization," Greenspan said in prepared testimony to the House Banking Committee.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Wednesday sidestepped the controversial question of whether banks should be allowed to merge with commercial companies, instead offering Congress two proposals -- one that would allow such combinations, the other that would not.
Greenspan said the Fed had turned more cautious about such proposals in part because of uncertainty about how they would affect the U.S. financial system.

In his prepared testimony, the Fed chief broadly endorsed a more modest bank reform plan put forward by House Banking Committee Chairman Jim Leach, a Republican from Iowa. That plan would give new powers to banks by allowing them to affiliate with securities firms and insurance companies.
"The (Fed) Board strongly supports the approach to financial modernization (in the Leach bill)," Greenspan said.

Greenspan said that the Fed has only one reservation about the Leach bill -- its provision that would allow operating subsidiaries of banks to engage in some financial activities not permittted to their parent.
The central bank opposes that provision because it fears that would increase the direct risks faced by the parent bank.
"We are concerned that conducting securities and similar activities as principal in subsidiaries of U.S. banks does not create sufficient distance from the bank," Greenspan said.

In his prepared testimony, Greenspan made a strong pitch for continued Fed surveillance of large banks and urged lawmakers not to undermine the central bank's powers in that area in their drive to modernize the financial system.

"Regardless of how restructuring is addressed, the Congress (should) not impair the ability of the Federal Reserve to monitor large banking organizations and respond effectively to systemic crises," he said.

However, the Fed Board, anticipating that some sort of financial modernization legislation will be passed, is considering alternative approaches to evaluating the capital adequacy of financial conglomerates whose main business is not banking, Greenspan said.
